slides.title: Scale Drawings
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: one number every length is multiplied by — the scale factor.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the lesson in miniature: a scale is a ratio, and the first move is always to read it per 1. Two minutes silent, then reveal; one sentence of reteach at most.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the figure and the line.
slides.note: Two rectangles, 6 by 4 and 9 by 6. Divide each copy side by its original side: 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5 and 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 — the same number both times, and that is what makes it a copy. **Say:** a scale factor is the one number every length is multiplied by; if two sides give different numbers, it is not a scale copy.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: The direction is fixed all unit: copy ÷ original. 10 → 4 is k = 0.4, and 0.4 is a perfectly good scale factor — the copy is smaller. The guide's named error is answering 2.5 here, the other way round. **Say:** k under 1 shrinks; k over 1 enlarges; k = 1 is the same size.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: From the original to the copy, multiply; from the copy back to the original, divide. On a map the scale is a k with units on it — 1 in : 20 mi means multiply inches by 20 to get miles, and divide miles by 20 to get inches. **Say:** multiply to go to the copy, divide to come back.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which side matches which before anyone divides: 15 matches 6, 10 matches 4.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 and 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5: the same k from both pairs, so it is a copy and k = 2.5. A board with 0.4 divided the other way; one with 9 subtracted.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: k = 1.5 from both pairs (9 ÷ 6 and 12 ÷ 8). Same structure, its own numbers. A board with ⅔ divided original by copy.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Use a scale on a map.
slides.note: Ask what the scale says per 1 inch before anyone multiplies.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Every inch is 20 miles, so 3.5 inches is 3.5 × 20 = 70 miles. A board with 0.175 divided.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 63 km: 4.2 × 15. A board with 0.28 divided.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.note: The boundary board: the one measurement a scale factor leaves alone. IXL's WEA asks for a missing angle, and the answer is always the angle you were given. On a split, hold up a small and a large square: four right angles each.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
